cluster.name: Shillong-Cherrapunji
cluster.summary: The Khasi Hills circuit: Shillong's colonial hill-station core, the Sohra (Cherrapunji) plateau with its waterfalls and limestone caves, and the living root bridges of the southern escarpment. Among the wettest inhabited places on earth, so weather drives the plan here more than anywhere else in India.
cluster.intercity_hub: Shillong Airport (SHL) / Guwahati Airport (GAU), 3.5 hours by road

attractions.name: Nohkalikai Falls
attractions.summary: India's tallest plunge waterfall at around 340 m, dropping into a turquoise plunge pool below the Sohra plateau.
attractions.history: The name comes from a Khasi legend about a woman named Ka Likai who, discovering a terrible truth about her second husband, threw herself from the cliff - 'Noh ka Likai' means 'the leap of Likai'. The falls are fed entirely by rainwater collected on the plateau above, which is why their volume varies enormously between seasons.
attractions.significance: Nohkalikai is the tallest plunge waterfall in India and the defining landscape image of the Sohra plateau. Because it is rain-fed rather than river-fed, it demonstrates directly how the region's extreme rainfall shapes its geography.
interesting_facts: The drop is approximately 340 metres in a single plunge.
The plunge pool takes on a distinct green-blue colour in the dry season.
The falls are entirely rain-fed and reduce to a thin ribbon in late winter.
In heavy monsoon the viewpoint is frequently in cloud and the falls are invisible.
attractions.accessibility_notes: The upper viewing terrace is reachable from the car park on a short paved path and gives the main view. Lower viewpoints require descending steep steps.
attractions.dress_code: Waterproof layer and non-slip footwear - the viewpoint is often wet even outside monsoon.
attractions.photography_policy: Personal photography permitted; drones require local permission.
local_customs: Cloud can obscure the falls entirely within minutes - allow flexibility.
Do not cross the safety barriers; the cliff edge is sheer and wet.
Meghalaya is a Sixth Schedule area - respect local community rules at all sites.

schedule.note: Viewpoint gate hours; visibility depends entirely on cloud

attractions.verification_note: Gate hours and entry charges are set locally and change - verify before visiting.

attractions.name: Double Decker Living Root Bridge, Nongriat
attractions.summary: A two-tier bridge grown over decades from living rubber-fig roots, reached by a demanding descent of roughly 3,500 steps.
attractions.history: The Khasi and Jaintia communities have trained the aerial roots of Ficus elastica across streams for centuries, guiding them along betel-nut trunks until they root on the far bank. A bridge takes fifteen to thirty years to become usable and then strengthens rather than decays with age. The Nongriat double-decker is the best known example.
attractions.significance: Living root bridges are a genuinely unique piece of vernacular bio-engineering: infrastructure that grows stronger over time and requires no material inputs. They are on India's UNESCO tentative list. Nongriat's is the only widely accessible two-tier example.
interesting_facts: Mature bridges can carry fifty people at once and last several hundred years.
The descent and return involve roughly 3,500 steps each way.
Bridges are grown, not built - they take fifteen to thirty years to become usable.
The village of Nongriat has no road access; everything arrives on foot.
attractions.accessibility_notes: Approximately 3,500 uneven concrete and stone steps down and the same back up, plus two steel suspension bridges. This is a strenuous half-day trek. Not accessible, and unsuitable for anyone with knee, heart or breathing conditions.
attractions.dress_code: Proper trekking shoes with grip, quick-dry clothing, rain layer. Leeches are common in wet months - carry salt or repellent.
attractions.photography_policy: Personal photography permitted. Ask before photographing villagers.
local_customs: Start by 07:00 - the return climb in afternoon heat is far harder.
Carry your own water and snacks; village shops are small.
Pay the community entry fee; it funds path maintenance.
Do not swim where villagers draw drinking water.
Local guides can be hired at Tyrna and are recommended.

schedule.note: Last safe start for the return climb is mid-morning

attractions.verification_note: Trail condition, fees and guide availability are managed by the village community and change - verify locally before setting out.

attractions.name: Mawsmai Cave
attractions.summary: A lit limestone cave with a 150 m walk-through passage of stalactites, narrow squeezes and low headroom.
attractions.history: The cave is part of the extensive limestone karst system of the southern Khasi Hills, formed by rainwater dissolving Eocene limestone over millions of years. A short section was lit and made walkable for visitors; the wider system extends far beyond the tourist route.
attractions.significance: Mawsmai is the most accessible of Meghalaya's caves and gives a direct sense of the karst landscape that the region's rainfall has carved. Meghalaya contains some of the longest cave systems in the subcontinent, most of them explored only in recent decades.
interesting_facts: Only about 150 metres of the system is open to visitors.
Several passages narrow enough that visitors must turn sideways or crouch.
The limestone here is Eocene, laid down when this was a shallow sea.
Meghalaya's caves include some of the longest surveyed systems in South Asia.
attractions.accessibility_notes: The passage involves steps, wet uneven rock, low headroom and sections narrow enough to require squeezing through. Not accessible, and unsuitable for anyone with claustrophobia or mobility limits.
attractions.dress_code: Non-slip footwear essential; clothes that can get wet and muddy.
attractions.photography_policy: Personal photography permitted; the passage is narrow so tripods are impractical.
local_customs: The passage is one-way - do not turn back against the flow.
Can flood after heavy rain and is closed at short notice.
Queues build sharply at midday.
attractions.verification_note: The cave closes without notice after heavy rain - verify before visiting.

attractions.name: Seven Sisters Falls (Nohsngithiang)
attractions.summary: A seven-segment waterfall plunging around 315 m off the southern escarpment, visible only when the rains are running.
attractions.history: Also called Nohsngithiang or Mawsmai Falls, the cascade splits into seven distinct streams as it drops from the limestone cliff edge toward the plains of Bangladesh. It is entirely seasonal and rain-dependent.
attractions.significance: The falls mark the exact line where the Khasi Hills drop away to the Sylhet plain - the escarpment that forces monsoon air upward and produces the region's record rainfall. On a clear day the Bangladesh plains are visible from the viewpoint.
interesting_facts: The seven separate streams give the falls their English name.
The drop is roughly 315 metres.
The falls run only in and shortly after the monsoon; by February they can be dry.
On a clear day the plains of Bangladesh are visible from the viewpoint.
attractions.accessibility_notes: The viewpoint terrace is a short level walk from the parking area and is usable with a wheelchair in dry conditions.
attractions.dress_code: Waterproof layer; the viewpoint is exposed and often windy.
local_customs: Cloud frequently hides the falls entirely - there is no refund and no guarantee.
Stay behind the barriers.
attractions.verification_note: Flow is entirely seasonal and visibility is cloud-dependent - verify conditions locally before visiting.

attractions.name: Mawlynnong Village
attractions.summary: A Khasi village known for community-run cleanliness, bamboo waste baskets on every lane and a living root bridge nearby.
attractions.history: Mawlynnong is a matrilineal Khasi village that organised a community sanitation system long before it drew attention, with every household responsible for a section of lane and a total ban on plastic and smoking in public. A 2003 magazine feature described it as the cleanest village in Asia, and tourism followed.
attractions.significance: The village is a working example of community-managed public space under Meghalaya's Sixth Schedule autonomy, where village durbars hold real authority. Khasi society is matrilineal - property and clan name pass through the youngest daughter - which visitors can see reflected in household organisation.
interesting_facts: Conical bamboo waste baskets are placed along every lane and emptied by rotation.
Khasi society is matrilineal: children take the mother's clan name and the youngest daughter inherits.
A bamboo sky-viewing platform gives a view over the plains of Bangladesh.
A living root bridge at nearby Riwai is a short, easy walk - a good alternative to the Nongriat trek.
attractions.accessibility_notes: The main village lanes are paved and mostly level and can be navigated with assistance. The sky-view platform is a bamboo tower with steep ladders and is not accessible; the Riwai root bridge involves a short descent of steps.
attractions.dress_code: Modest dress; this is a residential village, not a resort.
attractions.photography_policy: Ask before photographing residents or entering house compounds.
local_customs: Do not litter or smoke in public - both are actively enforced by the community.
Pay the village entry fee; it funds maintenance.
Homes are private property - stay on public lanes unless invited.
Sunday is a day of church attendance; the village is quieter and some services close.

schedule.note: Village is residential; visitor facilities keep daytime hours

attractions.verification_note: Community-set fees change - verify on arrival.

attractions.name: Elephant Falls
attractions.summary: A three-tier waterfall a short drive from Shillong, with stepped viewing platforms at each level.
attractions.history: The Khasi name is Ka Kshaid Lai Pateng Khohsiew - 'the three-step waterfall'. British visitors named it Elephant Falls after a rock at its base thought to resemble an elephant; that rock was destroyed in the 1897 Assam earthquake, but the English name stuck.
attractions.significance: Elephant Falls is the most accessible waterfall in the Shillong area and a useful contingency when Sohra is under cloud, since it sits at a lower elevation and remains visible more often.
interesting_facts: The elephant-shaped rock that gave the falls their English name was destroyed in the 1897 earthquake.
The Khasi name simply means 'three-step waterfall'.
Each of the three tiers has its own viewing platform.
The lowest tier is the tallest and the busiest for photographs.
attractions.accessibility_notes: The uppermost tier is reachable on a short level path from the car park. Reaching the lower tiers requires descending steep, often wet stone steps with handrails.
attractions.dress_code: Non-slip footwear - the steps are permanently damp.
local_customs: Steps are slippery even in dry weather - hold the rails.
Flow reduces substantially in late winter.
attractions.verification_note: Entry charges are set locally and change - verify before visiting.

attractions.name: Shillong Peak
attractions.summary: At 1,965 m the highest point in the Khasi Hills, giving a panorama over Shillong when the cloud lifts.
attractions.history: The peak is sacred in Khasi tradition as the abode of U Shulong, the guardian deity of the Khasi people, and a small shrine is maintained near the summit. The viewpoint sits within an Indian Air Force station, which is why access is controlled and photography restricted.
attractions.significance: Shillong Peak is both the region's highest viewpoint and a living sacred site. Its position inside a defence installation makes it one of the few Indian viewpoints where identity documents are required for entry.
interesting_facts: At 1,965 m it is the highest point in the Khasi Hills.
The peak is associated with U Shulong, the Khasi guardian deity.
Access runs through an Air Force station and identity documents are checked.
Photography is restricted to the designated viewpoint only.
attractions.accessibility_notes: Vehicles reach close to the viewing terrace, which is largely level; a few steps lead to the highest platform.
attractions.dress_code: Warm layers - it is markedly colder and windier than Shillong town.
attractions.photography_policy: Photography is permitted only at the designated viewpoint. Do not photograph the Air Force installation, personnel or approach road.
local_customs: Carry government photo identity for the security check.
The viewpoint may close at short notice for operational reasons.
Cloud regularly removes the view entirely.

schedule.note: Access controlled by the Air Force station; may close without notice

attractions.verification_note: Access is at the discretion of the Air Force station and can be withdrawn - verify before setting out.

attractions.name: Don Bosco Museum of Indigenous Cultures
attractions.summary: Seven floors documenting the tribal cultures of all eight Northeast states, with a rooftop skywalk over Shillong.
attractions.history: Opened in 2001 by the Salesians of Don Bosco, the museum was created to document and preserve the material culture of Northeast India's indigenous communities, drawing on decades of missionary field collection across the region.
attractions.significance: This is the most comprehensive single collection covering all eight Northeast states, with seventeen galleries on housing, agriculture, weaponry, textiles, music and religion. For anyone travelling in the region it is by far the most efficient way to understand its ethnic diversity.
interesting_facts: The building has seven floors and seventeen galleries arranged as a spiral route.
A rooftop skywalk gives a 360-degree view over Shillong.
The collection covers all eight Northeast states, not only Meghalaya.
It is fully indoor, making it the best contingency when the weather closes in.
attractions.accessibility_notes: A lift serves the main floors, but the spiral gallery route and the rooftop skywalk involve stairs and ramps that may be difficult for wheelchair users. Ask staff about the accessible route on arrival.
attractions.photography_policy: Photography inside the galleries is generally restricted; the skywalk is usually permitted.
local_customs: Bags must be deposited at reception.
Allow at least ninety minutes - the route is long.
attractions.verification_note: Sunday closure and ticket rates change - verify before visiting.

attractions.name: Ward's Lake (Pollock's Lake)
attractions.summary: A horseshoe-shaped artificial lake in central Shillong with a wooden arched bridge, botanical garden and boating.
attractions.history: Created in the 1890s during the tenure of Sir William Ward, Chief Commissioner of Assam, the lake was landscaped as a public garden at the centre of the new hill station. Its wooden footbridge across the narrow point is the most photographed structure in Shillong.
attractions.significance: Ward's Lake is the surviving core of Shillong's colonial hill-station planning and remains the city's principal public garden, ringed by the botanical garden and government buildings.
interesting_facts: The lake was excavated by prison labour in the 1890s.
Its arched wooden bridge is the standard image of central Shillong.
Pedal boats operate on the lake in fair weather.
An adjoining botanical garden holds native Khasi Hills flora including orchids.
attractions.accessibility_notes: Paved level paths circle the lake with benches throughout; the bridge has a gentle ramp. One of the most accessible outdoor spaces in the region.
attractions.dress_code: No restriction; carry a rain layer.
local_customs: Feeding the fish is a local pastime; feed is sold at the gate.
Boating suspends in rain.

schedule.note: Typically closed on Tuesdays for maintenance

attractions.verification_note: Weekly closure day and rates change - verify before visiting.

attractions.name: Arwah Lumshynna Cave
attractions.summary: A limestone cave with visible marine fossils in its walls, reached through a short forest walk.
attractions.history: Arwah Lumshynna was opened to visitors more recently than Mawsmai and is set within a protected forest reserve. Its walls preserve fossils of marine crustaceans and fish embedded in the limestone, evidence that the Khasi Hills were once seabed.
attractions.significance: Unlike Mawsmai, Arwah is valued for what its rock contains rather than its formations: the visible fossil record makes the region's geological history directly legible. The approach through forest also makes it a more complete outing.
interesting_facts: Fossilised marine organisms are visible in the cave walls.
The approach is a walk of several hundred metres through reserve forest.
The cave is generally less crowded than Mawsmai.
Lighting is installed but a torch is still useful.
attractions.accessibility_notes: The forest approach includes steps and a descent; the cave floor is wet and uneven. Not accessible.
attractions.dress_code: Non-slip footwear; the path and cave floor are wet.
local_customs: Do not remove or damage fossils.
The cave can flood after heavy rain.
attractions.verification_note: Closes after heavy rain; fees set locally - verify before visiting.

attractions.name: Mawphlang Sacred Forest
attractions.summary: A community-protected sacred grove where nothing may be removed, preserving old-growth Khasi Hills forest and monoliths.
attractions.history: Law Lyngdoh Mawphlang has been protected by the Lyngdoh clan for centuries under Khasi religious law, which forbids removing anything from the grove - not a leaf, a stone or a fallen branch. Standing monoliths at the entrance mark clan ritual sites. The taboo has preserved a fragment of the forest that once covered the plateau.
attractions.significance: Sacred groves are among the oldest functioning conservation institutions in the world, and Mawphlang is the best documented in Meghalaya. Botanists use it as a reference for what the pre-agricultural Khasi Hills vegetation looked like, including rare orchids, epiphytes and medicinal plants found nowhere else nearby.
interesting_facts: Removing anything from the grove, even a dead leaf, is forbidden by religious law.
Standing monoliths at the entrance mark traditional clan sacrifice sites.
The forest floor holds a metre-deep humus layer built up over centuries.
A local guide from the community is mandatory and explains the ritual context.
attractions.accessibility_notes: Forest floor is uneven with roots, mud and fallen wood that cannot be cleared because of the taboo. Not accessible.
attractions.dress_code: Closed shoes with grip; the ground is permanently damp.
attractions.photography_policy: Personal photography permitted; ask the guide before photographing ritual sites.
local_customs: Take nothing out of the grove - this is a religious prohibition, not a request.
A community guide is compulsory.
Do not litter or eat inside the grove.
Speak quietly; the grove is a place of worship.
attractions.verification_note: Guide fees and hours are set by the community and change - verify on arrival.

attractions.name: Police Bazar
attractions.summary: Shillong's central market and social hub, known for Khasi textiles, cane goods and a dense street-food scene.
attractions.history: Police Bazar developed as the commercial centre of the colonial hill station and remains the focal point of Shillong life. Its side lanes hold the traditional Khasi markets alongside modern retail.
attractions.significance: The market is where the region's produce and crafts converge - Khasi shawls, cane and bamboo work, Meghalaya's distinctive honey and the local Lakadong turmeric. It is also the practical base for onward transport across the state.
interesting_facts: Lakadong turmeric from Jaintia Hills has one of the highest curcumin contents in the world.
Khasi cane and bamboo craft is sold directly by producers in the side lanes.
Most shops close early by mainland Indian standards, and much of the market shuts on Sundays.
Shared taxis to most Meghalaya destinations depart from the surrounding streets.
attractions.accessibility_notes: Main streets have footpaths but they are narrow and crowded; side lanes are uneven with steps.
attractions.dress_code: No restriction; carry a rain layer.
local_customs: Most shops close on Sundays.
Shops shut noticeably earlier than in mainland Indian cities - by around 19:00.
Bargaining is modest here compared with north India.
attractions.verification_note: Shop hours and Sunday closures vary - verify before visiting.
